summary: the file is not a table the reader can follow (a quote never closed, text after a closing quote, a cell too long, semicolons for commas), has no event_type column or has a header and no rows, so nothing in it was checked
fix: Save the events as CSV with commas or TSV with tabs, a header row and one row for each event (docs/inputs.md); fix the line named.
own: Refusing a file that cannot be followed is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a tool that guessed would report on cells it did not read

summary: a column that the rows of a kind of event need is not in the header at all; it is reported once, at the header, and not for each row
fix: Add the column named to the spreadsheet and fill it for the rows that need it; docs/inputs.md lists every column.
own: Asking for these columns is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the columns and their names are the tool's own, because no regulation fixes them

summary: a column the tool does not read, often a misspelt name; nothing under it was checked
fix: Correct the name to a column of docs/inputs.md, or leave the column in if it is for your own use.
own: Reporting a column that is not read is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a misspelt name would otherwise hide a cell from every check

summary: two columns of the header have the same name once case and separators are ignored; only the first is read
fix: Keep one column of each name.
own: Refusing a column written twice is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; two readers could see two values

summary: a row with more or fewer cells than the header, which usually means a comma that is not in quotes; the row was left out of every other check
fix: Put a cell that holds a comma, a tab or a line end in double quotes, and write a quote inside it as two quotes.
own: Reporting a row of the wrong width is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; every cell after the extra one would be shifted and read as another column

summary: the file holds a private key, a seed or a mnemonic, under a column named for one or as a cell shaped like one; the tool never reads it and never shows it
fix: Remove the value from the file and from wherever the file was copied, treat it as exposed and move what it controls to a new key. A record of lots names lots, parties and quantities, never the key of an account.
own: Looking for keys and seeds is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a file that goes to a shared ledger project often sits next to wallets, and a report must never copy a secret into a log

summary: an event_type that is empty or is none of receive, produce, ship, assemble and scrap; the row was left out of the other checks
fix: Write one of "receive", "produce", "ship", "assemble" or "scrap" in the event_type column.
own: The list of five kinds of event is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the kinds and their names are the tool's own, kept small on purpose

summary: a cell that the kind of event needs is empty or a placeholder such as n/a: event_id, event_time, party, lot and quantity for every kind, the product for receive, produce and assemble, to_party for ship, input_lots for assemble; also a ship row whose from_party is not its party
fix: Fill the cell named from the business record the row comes from; docs/inputs.md says what each kind of event needs.
own: Asking for these cells is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a chain of lots cannot be followed through a row that does not say which lot, who or when

summary: a quantity that is not a plain positive number: zero, negative, with a thousands separator, with an exponent, text, or with more than 40 digits
fix: Write the quantity as a plain number above zero, such as 25 or 12.5, with no unit in the cell.
own: Asking for a plain positive number is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a quantity of zero or one that is text cannot be added up or compared

summary: a quantity with no unit in the unit column
fix: Give the unit with the quantity, such as kg, pieces or litres.
own: Asking for the unit is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; quantities are added up and compared only in one unit, so a quantity with no unit can be checked against nothing

summary: an entry of input_lots that is not written lot:quantity:unit, with a quantity that is not a plain number above zero; the event is not compared with its inputs
fix: Write each input as lot:quantity:unit and separate the entries with semicolons, such as RM-1:5:kg;RM-2:2:kg.
own: The form lot:quantity:unit is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the tool needs the quantity of each input to compare an event with its inputs
context: GS1 EPCIS has an event type for an event that uses input items or lots and makes output items or lots, and a produce or assemble row with input_lots is the same idea in a spreadsheet; this tool does not read EPCIS and does not check conformance to it.

summary: an event_time that is not a date, names a day that does not exist, has a time with no time zone, or is written as a date of the United States
fix: Write the time as YYYY-MM-DD, or as YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss with a time zone, Z or +hh:mm.
own: Reading only dates written one way is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the order of month and day in other forms is ambiguous, and the order of events depends on the time

summary: an event_time later than the moment given with --now (a day alone is allowed one day more, for the time zones of the world); without --now the check does not run
fix: Correct the time or the clock of the system that wrote it; an event cannot be recorded before it took place.
own: Refusing a time from the future is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the tool reads no clock, so the moment is the one given with --now

summary: the outputs of a produce or assemble event add up to more than its inputs in the same unit, above the --yield-tolerance percent; the rows of one event_id, kind, party and time are one event
fix: Check the quantities against the work order, name the inputs that were left out, or set --yield-tolerance if a gain such as added water is expected.
own: A mass balance is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a process that makes more than it uses has an input that is not written down, and a warning leaves room for added ingredients
context: GS1 EPCIS has an event type for an event that uses input items or lots and makes output items or lots, and a produce or assemble row with input_lots is the same idea in a spreadsheet; this tool does not read EPCIS and does not check conformance to it.

summary: a note: the inputs and outputs of an event, or the quantities of one lot, are in different units, so the tool cannot compare them
fix: Use one unit for the lot and for the event, or accept that this event and this lot are not checked for quantity.
own: Comparing only in one unit is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a conversion between units belongs to a recipe or a product, which the file does not carry

summary: an input lot of a produce or assemble row that no receive or produce row of the file holds, or that is received or made only after it is used
fix: Add the receive or produce row of the lot, correct the lot code, or correct the times; a lot has to exist before it is used.
own: Following each input back to a row is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a lot that appears out of nowhere cannot be traced back
context: GS1 EPCIS has an event type for an event that uses input items or lots and makes output items or lots, and a produce or assemble row with input_lots is the same idea in a spreadsheet; this tool does not read EPCIS and does not check conformance to it.

summary: the quantities of a lot that a party ships, scraps or uses add up to more than that party received or made of it, in the same unit, with exact sums; a lot that no row receives or makes and that is shipped or scrapped counts as held in a quantity of zero
fix: Check the quantities of the row named, and whether a receive or produce row of the lot is missing from the file.
own: Adding up what a party holds of a lot and what leaves it is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a party cannot give more than it has, and a file that holds only some of the rows can show this by mistake; the sums are kept for each party because a ship and its receive are one movement of the same material

summary: the same serial number in two produce or assemble rows; a serial number names one unit and is made once
fix: Give each unit its own serial number, or delete the repeated row.
own: Treating a serial number as unique in the file is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; if your serial numbers repeat from one product to the next, put the product in front of them
context: Work on digital product passports speaks of data at the level of a batch or of an item, so a chain of lots and serial numbers that holds together is useful input to that work; this tool checks no passport and does not say what a passport needs.

summary: the same serial number on two different lots or two different products
fix: Correct the lot or the product of the row named, or give the units different serial numbers.
own: Treating a serial number as one unit is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a unit is in one lot and is one product
context: Work on digital product passports speaks of data at the level of a batch or of an item, so a chain of lots and serial numbers that holds together is useful input to that work; this tool checks no passport and does not say what a passport needs.

summary: a lot is shipped from A to B and the next event on it is by C, not B; or B ships, scraps or uses it without a receive; or a receive names another sender than the ship; or a party acts on a lot that another party last held
fix: Add the missing receive or ship row, or correct the party in the row named.
own: Following a lot from party to party is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a lot that changes hands without a record cannot be traced through the gap, and a file that holds only some of the rows can show this by mistake

summary: a lot is received before it is shipped, or shipped or scrapped before the first row that receives or makes it
fix: Correct the time of the row named; a lot cannot arrive before it is sent.
own: Reading the times along the custody chain is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; events of one lot should not go back in time

summary: a note: a receive row for a lot that no ship row of the file sends to that party; a file of one party holds the receipts of lots shipped by others
fix: If the file is meant to hold both sides of every move, add the ship row; if it holds one party, no change is needed.
own: Matching a receive with a ship is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; each party keeps its own records, so this is a note

summary: a note: a ship row for a lot that no receive row of the file takes in at the party it is sent to; the recipient keeps its own records
fix: If the file is meant to hold both sides of every move, add the receive row; if it holds one party, no change is needed.
own: Matching a ship with a receive is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; the recipient keeps its own records, so this is a note

summary: a lot that is, directly or through other lots, one of its own inputs
fix: Correct the input_lots of the row named; a lot is made from lots that existed before it.
own: Refusing a loop in the genealogy is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a trace backward from a lot in a loop never ends
context: GS1 EPCIS has an event type for an event that uses input items or lots and makes output items or lots, and a produce or assemble row with input_lots is the same idea in a spreadsheet; this tool does not read EPCIS and does not check conformance to it.

summary: a row whose cells are all the same as an earlier row, which counts one event twice; it is left out of the other checks
fix: Delete the repeated row, or correct the cell that should differ.
own: Looking for repeated rows is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; a repeated row doubles the quantity of a lot

summary: the same event_id on two rows that are not one event; rows of one produce or assemble event with the same kind, party and time may share an event_id
fix: Give each event its own event_id.
own: Asking for a unique event_id is a best practice of this tool; no regulation sets it; an event that is named twice cannot be pointed at
